record.paper_title: Open problems on countable dense homogeneity
record.context_brief: finite product threshold from non-CDH to CDH
record.original_question: For which natural numbers n does there exist a space X such that X^i is not countable dense homogeneous for every i <= n, but X^(n+1) is countable dense homogeneous; and can such an X be chosen to be a continuum?

evidence.quote: Problem 16 (Medini [58]). For which n ∈ ω is there a CDH space X such that Xi is not CDH for all i ≤ n while Xn+1 is CDH? Can X be a continuum?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A separable topological space $Y$ is called countable dense homogeneous (CDH) if for any two countable dense subsets $D_1, D_2 \subseteq Y$ there exists a homeomorphism $h \colon Y \to Y$ with $h(D_1) = D_2$. A continuum is a compact connected metrizable space.

Determine the set of natural numbers $n \geq 1$ for which there exists a topological space $X$ such that:
(i) $X^i$ is not countable dense homogeneous for every integer $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq n$, and
(ii) $X^{n+1}$ is countable dense homogeneous.

In addition, determine for which such $n$ the space $X$ can be chosen to be a continuum.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) has produced zero-dimensional metrizable CDH spaces $X$ with $X^2$ not CDH (under Martin's Axiom) and has studied CDH in large products of Polish spaces, but no source located resolves the precise threshold question of finding, for each $n$, a space whose powers $X^i$ ($i\le n$) all fail to be CDH while $X^{n+1}$ is CDH, nor the continuum version. The problem appears to remain open.
